analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug companies from paying generic rivals to keep cheaper competition off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill won approval from the Senate Judiciary Committee with bipartisan support in March 2023 and sat on the Senate calendar, but never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic or biosimilar maker challenges a brand-name drug's patents, the two companies sometimes settle with a 'pay-for-delay' deal: the brand-name company pays the challenger to stay out of the market longer. This bill tells the Federal Trade Commission to treat those deals as presumptively anticompetitive and lets it impose penalties, including taking away a generic maker's prized 180-day exclusivity window. Cheaper generic and biosimilar versions of drugs would reach patients sooner, lowering prices for patients, insurers, and taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need drugs where cheaper versions are being delayed by settlement payments; employers and insurers who pay drug bills; and taxpayers, since federal programs like Medicare cover a large share of retail drug spending.

how_it_helps.text: Presumes that a patent settlement is anticompetitive if the generic or biosimilar filer receives anything of value and agrees to stay out of the market for a period of time [S2] [S4].

The bill's own findings note that generics average discounts of 80 to 85 percent off brand prices and account for 88 percent of prescriptions but only 28 percent of drug spending, so faster generic entry means large savings [S4].
Federal dollars cover over 40 percent of the roughly $325 billion spent on retail prescription drugs, so delayed generics inflate taxpayer costs directly [S4].
Gives the FTC enforcement power with civil penalties up to triple the value gained, and strips a violating generic maker of its 180-day marketing exclusivity [S2] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would lose the ability to extend monopolies by paying generic challengers, and generic makers would lose a lucrative option to accept payment instead of launching their product.

drawbacks.text: Not every settlement with value to a generic maker is bad for consumers: deals like authorized generics or co-marketing arrangements can bring a cheaper product to market sooner. The bill tries to handle this by exempting entry-date agreements, capped litigation-cost payments (up to $7.5 million in 2023, indexed thereafter), and covenants not to sue, but the bright-line presumption could still chill genuinely procompetitive settlements and invite litigation over the exemptions [S4].

The penalty of forfeiting a generic maker's 180-day first-filer exclusivity cuts both ways: it deters collusion, but taking exclusivity away can let other generic makers jump in, which helps consumers yet may make first filers more reluctant to challenge patents at all [S2] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is sound: the largest cost falls on companies whose revenue depends on delaying cheaper competition, and the exemptions are designed to keep legitimate settlements available. The main risk is that the presumption and penalties make companies so cautious that they litigate to the end instead of settling early, which can itself delay generic entry. On balance the public benefit of faster, cheaper drug access outweighs that risk.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate's calendar of bills awaiting floor action in March 2023, but the majority leader never brought it up for a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill with a bipartisan list of cosponsors including Republican Senator Grassley in January 2023 [S1] [S4].
The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably on February 9, 2023, and it was reported to the full Senate with an amendment on March 1, 2023 [S6].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 20, on March 1, 2023, and no further action was ever taken [S6].
With 10 cosponsors split between the parties (7 Democrats, 3 Republicans), the bill had bipartisan backing but never reached a floor vote in the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: they kept the ability to settle patent suits by paying generic challengers to stay out of the market, and patients and taxpayers kept paying brand-name prices where those deals delay cheaper generics.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the Judiciary Committee process.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the lead Republican cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably out of committee and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: 10 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of 49 Senate Republicans

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; it sat on the calendar for nearly two years until the Congress ended.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Long opposed legislation restricting pay-for-delay settlements, arguing such deals can speed generic entry and that the bill would invite more litigation.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and the bill was reported out of committee without any recorded opposition vote.

industries.note: Pay-for-delay settlements let these companies extend monopoly pricing by compensating the generic challenger; the bill makes those deals presumptively unlawful and adds penalties up to triple the value gained. Every year a cheaper generic or biosimilar is delayed, patients, insurers, and Medicare pay brand-name prices.

These companies gain a faster route to market and lose the option of taking a brand-name payment to stay out. The bill also threatens them with forfeiture of the 180-day first-filer exclusivity if they collude, which cuts against some of their own deal-making incentives but pushes toward the competition consumers want.

industries.industry: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Faster generic and biosimilar entry lowers drug costs these payers absorb, and their interest runs alongside patients' — though PBMs also profit on brand-price spreads, so savings flow through imperfectly.
